item.title: Is Your Exposure Management Platform Leaving You Exposed? Five Tests to Find Out (2026)
item.description:
A critical finding can move through several security tools and still leave the organization exposed. 

The vulnerability has a severity score, and a ticket has reached the queue. Progress then depends on information the finding may lack: who owns the system, whether attackers can reach it, what protection exists, and how a change could affect the business. 

Each missing detail creates another investigation, another handoff, and another delay. 

An exposure management platform should connect discovery with a clear priority, an appropriate response, and evidence that protection has improved. 

Continuous threat exposure management (CTEM) connects this work through scoping, discovery, prioritization, validation, and mobilization. These five tests establish whether a platform can support that process across infrastructure, identities, sensitive data, and external threats.

Security teams often have several records of the same asset. A cloud platform identifies an instance, an endpoint tool records its hostname, and an inventory lists an owner who has changed roles. 

Cyber asset attack surface management (CAASM) connects those records, helping reveal stale information, missing ownership, and protection gaps. 

The resulting view needs enough detail to support action: the asset’s owner, business purpose, assessment history, and security coverage. A system with no reported vulnerabilities should be distinguishable from one never assessed. 

Disagreements between sources also need to remain visible. If an endpoint tool reports an active server while the inventory marks it retired, source records and update times help teams resolve the conflict. 

Figure 1. CAASM connects source records with asset ownership, security coverage, and exposure context.

External discovery adds another perspective. External attack surface management (EASM) helps uncover what assets make accessible from the outside, including shadow IT, forgotten subdomains, and exposed services that internal tools never see. 

EASM and CAASM work best together: CAASM maps what you know you own, while EASM validates that picture from the attacker’s point of view and surfaces what’s missing. Every unmanaged asset EASM finds can be fed back into CAASM, closing coverage gaps and giving each asset an owner. EASM also covers brand exposure, extending discovery to phishing sites, fraudulent profiles, and brand impersonation, so the same external view that finds your unknown assets also finds the lookalikes attackers build to target your customers and employees. 

Read CAASM Was Never Meant to Stand Alone to see how asset intelligence supports the decisions and actions that follow discovery. 

2. Explain Which Exposures Require Action First 

Prioritization depends on understanding what an exposure actually puts at risk. A customer-facing application may carry the same severity score as an isolated development system while presenting very different business risk. 

Prioritization should connect: 

  • Reachability and exploitability: Whether attackers have a usable path to exploit the weakness. 
  • Threat activity: Whether attackers are targeting the vulnerability or technology. 
  • Business impact: What the system supports and what compromise could affect. 
  • Existing protection: Whether relevant controls cover the system and are enforced. 

Those conditions change. New exploitation activity may accelerate a response, while a disabled protection may invalidate an earlier assessment. 

External threats need similarly specific reasoning. A fraudulent support account approaching customers may require rapid disruption; an abandoned company profile may first need ownership review. 

See what the 2026 Exposure Gap Report reveals about prioritization and remediation performance. 

3. Validate the Exposure and the Proposed Response 

A clear priority can still stall when the system owner lacks confidence in the proposed change. 

Validation needs to establish what the exposure allows and how the response could affect operations. 

Identifying vulnerable software, confirming reachability, and demonstrating exploitability establish different things. A platform should distinguish observed evidence from analysis and untested assumptions. Attack-path relationships also need supporting evidence and clear limitations. 

The proposed response requires separate assessment. A patch may depend on application testing and a maintenance window. An intrusion prevention system protection may require observation in Detect mode before enforcement. 

Evidence should address the action’s scope, dependencies, false positives, performance impact, and recovery options. Following a proposed change through this assessment reveals what the platform establishes and what teams must investigate themselves. 

4. Carry Safe Remediation Through Existing Workflows 

Knowing what to fix first is great, but only if the fix happens quickly. The permanent patch often waits on testing, approval, and a maintenance window, and the exposure stays open the whole time. That’s true whether the weakness is on an internet-facing server or a phishing site targeting your customers. 

Speed comes from confidence. Teams hesitate when they can’t say what an action will touch. When the platform already knows the asset, its owner, the active threat, and the controls in place, that hesitation disappears. Many Check Point Exposure Management customers remediate safely within one hour, because the context is complete and the safety checks are built in. 

To test this, take one real finding and follow it from priority to protection: 

  • Owner: Is the right person assigned automatically? 
  • Safety: Is the action validated before it runs, including its impact and a way back? 
  • Execution: Does it run through the controls you already have, whether a virtual patch, a configuration change, or a takedown? 
  • Confirmation: Is the result verified, with the permanent fix still tracked? 

Interim protection buys time, but it shouldn’t replace the long term fix. 

Figure 2. Safe remediation connects observation, validation, action, and confirmation.

Speed holds up at scale. Between January 1 and October 26, 2026, an airline group completed more than 1,500 takedowns of profiles impersonating its airlines and support teams, combining analyst review with automated remediation. 

And when an action fails, the exposure should stay visible with a clear next step. 

Read Safe Remediation: Confident Remediation in Production to see how validation, execution, and confirmation work together. 

5. Show What Changed and What Remains 

A completed action needs evidence of the resulting state. 

A patch may miss unavailable systems. A policy update may exclude an intended asset. A takedown request may be accepted before the account disappears. 

Verification should establish whether the vulnerability remains, protection is enforced, or malicious content has been removed. Monitoring should identify recurrence. 

Reporting must distinguish removed vulnerabilities, interim mitigations, completed takedowns, and accepted risk. Each leaves different responsibilities outstanding. 

Mean time to remediate (MTTR) requires agreed starting points, completion criteria, and treatment of temporary protection. 

Tracking assignment, approval, execution, and verification separately reveals delays. 

Recurring findings, failed actions, and aging mitigations can expose operational problems another scan will not resolve. 

Apply the Tests Across Vendors 

Platforms approach these requirements from different foundations. The five tests provide a consistent basis for evaluating coverage, evidence, and action. 

Check Point Exposure Management combines internal asset intelligence, external discovery, threat intelligence, and brand protection with prioritization, exploitability validation, and safe remediation. It spans infrastructure weaknesses, phishing, and brand impersonation, supporting action through existing controls and takedown workflows. 

Bring Intelligence Through to Safe Action 

The five tests follow an exposure from discovery to a confirmed response. Each stage should give the next team enough reliable information to act while keeping unresolved work visible. 

Check Point Exposure Management carries asset and threat context into responses to vulnerabilities, control gaps, and external threats. Proposed actions are evaluated before enforcement, with approved responses coordinated through supported Check Point and third-party technologies. 

That connection helps organizations strengthen protection while accounting for production constraints and building on existing investments. It creates a traceable path from an identified exposure to an evaluated, implemented, and confirmed response.

item.title: ThreatsDay: Apache OFBiz RCE, DreamHost Breach, DeFi Site Hijacks + 17 More Stories (2026)
item.description:
How much damage can someone do without breaking much? Quite a lot, it seems. A stolen login can open doors across several systems. A trusted setting can be used to lock people out. Even a simple file copy can reach places it shouldn't. And while new tools are helping find security holes faster, some important systems are still taking months, sometimes over a year, to get patched. Not exactly a great match.

The stranger part is how little some attacks now need. Ransom demands without encrypted files. Fake websites that look real enough to steal money. AI tools picking up dangerous instructions while trying to help. Even the attackers are making mistakes in their own code.

This week's stories are a reminder that the biggest problems don't always come from clever tricks. Sometimes the easy way works just fine. Here's what else happened.

The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out.
  1. AI Accelerates Zero-Day Discovery
    NCSC Warns of AI-Enabled Attacks

    The U.K. National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) has warned that the widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has "almost certainly" led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities. "Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and have made patching a quicker process," NCSC said. "However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses. Additionally, an organisation’s internal patching and testing processes will need to evolve to meet the pace of accelerating vulnerability discovery. Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal."

  2. Critical Systems Face Prolonged Exposure
    Network Appliances Go More Than a Year Without Patches

    An analysis of roughly 383,000 CVEs disclosed from 1999 through September 2026 has found that the median time to patch a vulnerability exceeds a year for network appliances. About 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation. "The median vulnerability is patched in about two weeks on Windows workstations but in more than a month on Windows Servers," Microsoft said. "It stretches to 10+ weeks on Linux Servers and for applications running on macOS, and beyond a year on network appliances. That gap is the threat actor's window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest." The tech giant also said threat actors disproportionately target flaws that maximize impact and exposure and enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass.

  3. $4.5 Million Fraud Network Busted
    Investment Fraud Scheme Dismantled in Europe

    Authorities have arrested seven people allegedly involved in an investment fraud scheme that claimed potential victims in more than 50 countries, according to Europol. The operation caused estimated losses of at least $4.5 million. The "crime-as-a-service" offering was run by a company from Cyprus and Israel, and allegedly provided cybercrime groups with an assortment of trading websites and fraudulent call centers tasked with tricking victims into transferring their savings. These call centers operated from Albania, Kosovo, and North Macedonia. "More than 100 servers were seized and seven suspects arrested during coordinated action on 3 November 2026," Europol said. "Authorities searched 17 locations and seized servers, other evidence and assets." Like other fraudulent investment schemes, the operation leveraged deceptive advertisements to funnel people towards fraudulent investment platforms, promising them substantial, quick returns from cryptocurrency trading and foreign currencies. Although victims were encouraged to transfer a small amount, they displayed illusory gains to push them into transferring increasingly large sums. The operators resorted to delaying tactics to block payments when they attempted to withdraw their funds. "Behind seemingly legitimate platforms, supposed brokers used fictitious profits and sustained psychological pressure to persuade victims to invest more," Europol said. "Personal data collected through this process was sold to criminal groups operating call centers. Operators then contacted potential victims with supposed investment opportunities, turning their initial interest into repeated demands for money."

  4. $250K Bounty for Critical Cloud Flaws
    Google Expands Cloud Vulnerability Reward Program

    Google has expanded its Cloud Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) with a new top-tier reward for high-impact architectural security flaws, allowing researchers to earn $250,000 for Root-in-Cloud bugs, including tenant-isolation bypasses and complex cross-service logic flaws that let attackers gain full administrative control over arbitrary Google Cloud organizations. "To earn this premier reward, you must demonstrate full administrative control, the equivalent of 'roles/owner' or complete IAM control, over arbitrary Google Cloud organizations or projects with no prior access or special project setup," Google said. "Additionally, valid vulnerability reports demonstrating remote code execution (RCE) in underlying Google production infrastructure (Borg) or achieving root-in-prod will automatically be evaluated by the Google Cloud VRP panel for root-in-cloud eligibility."

  5. Edge Blocks Scam Notification Abuse
    Microsoft Takes on Notification Spam in Edge

    Microsoft has announced that its Edge browser will now automatically disable notifications from sites that push scam or scareware notifications, such as fake virus warnings or security alerts. "As of last month’s rollout of Edge 156, when Microsoft Defender SmartScreen or Scareware blocker detects a scam that was pushed through a notification, Edge will automatically disable notifications from the site that sent it," Microsoft said. "The next time Edge starts, an information bar explains what happened. If you believe a site was blocked incorrectly, you can review sites with blocked notifications and unblock them from Edge Settings, keeping you in control."

  6. University Cryptojacking Charges
    U.S. Charges Two Canadians for Hacking U.S. Universities

    Two Canadian men, Ryan James Roach, 35, and Mathiew James Stubbings, 41, have been indicted in the U.S. for hacking multiple U.S. universities and using the access to mine cryptocurrency. Both have been charged with conspiracy to obtain information from a protected computer and to cause damage to a protected computer, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentional damage to a protected computer, which carry a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. "Between June 2016, and December 2019, Roach and Stubbings conspired to engage in a scheme to hack into computers, steal login credentials, and secretly mine cryptocurrency for financial gain," the Justice Department said. "They used virtual private servers in multiple countries, which were registered under false names. These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials. Victims of the scheme included educational institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Massachusetts."

  7. Ransomware Extortion Without Encryption
    PAYLOAD Ransomware Weaponizes Active Directory GPO

    Cybersecurity researchers have detailed an encryptionless extortion attack involving PAYLOAD ransomware targeting a manufacturing organization in the Middle East. "The threat actor obtained domain admin-equivalent control of the organization’s Active Directory environment and authored a malicious Group Policy Object (GPO) named PAYLOAD, linking it at the domain root," Kaspersky said. "Through that single object, the actor delivered ransom notes, hijacked the desktop wallpaper and lock screen, enforced a logon banner, and disabled the local administrator account across every domain-joined Windows workstation — all without dropping a ransomware binary or encrypting any data. The only ransomware we found in this incident was a PAYLOAD sample targeting ESXi on Linux servers." The attack represents a convergence of two trends: Living-off-the-land abuse of trusted AD infrastructure and a surge in extortion-only incidents.

  8. AI Sandbox Escape Exposes Sensitive Files
    Docker Sandboxes Flaw Lets AI Agents Access and Overwrite Files Outside Isolated Workspaces

    A vulnerability impacting Docker Sandboxes (CVE-2026-103916) could have been exploited to bypass file access restrictions, potentially exposing cloud credentials and other sensitive files on a developer's machine through a routine copy command. "The command used to copy files between a sandbox and the developer's computer (sbx cp) does not enforce these access restrictions," Endor Labs said. "An agent can exploit this weakness using what is known as a symbolic link, essentially a shortcut that points to another file or folder. By placing a malicious shortcut inside an approved workspace, the agent can trick a subsequent copy command into accessing files outside the sandbox's approved boundaries." The issue has been addressed in Docker Sandboxes version 0.51.0.

  9. Smart TVs Keep Tracking After Opt-Out
    Does Opting Out of ACR Work?

    A new study has revealed that smart TVs running operating systems from Samsung, Vizio, and Roku continue to transmit data to automatic content recognition (ACR) endpoints even after users opt out of tracking in the devices' settings. "Opting out fully worked on only four operating systems. On Samsung and Vizio, traffic consistent with ACR kept flowing, and Roku's opt-out doesn't cover its own streaming service," according to a group of academics from Northeastern University. "VIDAA OS sends ACR data to servers run by Unruly over MQTT without encryption, so anyone on the network path between the TV and those servers can read it."

  10. Cryptographic Proof for AI Outputs
    Anthropic Unveils FlashProve Prototype

    Anthropic has revealed that it's working on an open-source system called FlashProve to cryptographically verify an AI response came from a given model. "FlashProve is a system for provable inference of large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models," Anthropic said. "FlashProve involves two parties: the model provider (the prover) and a user (the verifier). It is split into two phases: In the offline phase, the prover publishes a commitment to the model weights, which is a short fingerprint to pin down one exact choice of weights while the weights themselves remain hidden. The later inference claims will be checked against that commitment, i.e., the weight model committed to in this phase. In the online phase, upon requests from the verifier (i.e., prompts and the corresponding output tokens), the prover produces a proof file proving the following statement: The committed model produces these output tokens when evaluated. Anyone who holds the commitment, the prompt, and the reply can check it, without the weights and with limited compute power, and be convinced that the committed weights, run on this prompt, produce exactly these tokens."

  11. FTP and Webmail Credentials Exposed
    DreamHost Confirms Data Breach Exposing FTP Passwords and Webmail Credentials

    DreamHost has warned of a data breach after an unauthorized third party gained access to the server that runs its web-based File Manager at files.dreamhost.com between August and October 23, 2026. "The unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in that software and was able to access the FTP/SFTP usernames and passwords of individuals who logged into this File Manager between approximately August 2026 and October 23, 2026," the company said. "The unauthorized third party was also able to reach certain webmail systems, which may have exposed the session information (the data that keeps a user signed in, including session credentials) of a limited number of webmail users. We believe this was a deliberate attack, and our team worked around the clock to contain it." DreamHost said the attacker may have accessed the credentials used to access the File Manager or webmail, along with the contents of emails and files in the FTP/SFTP server. There is no evidence that the attacker accessed control panel login information or customer billing details.

  12. Pre-Auth RCE and Account Takeover
    Critical Apache OFBiz Flaws Allow Unauthenticated RCE and Admin Account Takeover

    The maintainers of Apache OFBiz have addressed 46 security flaws, including CVE-2026-68524, which could result in pre-authentication remote code execution, and CVE-2026-109928, which enables full account takeover due to an incorrect authentication algorithm implementation. The issues have been patched in Apache OFBiz 24.09.08.

  13. Ransomware Encryption Flaws Exposed
    HYFLOCK Ransomware's Weaknesses Exposed

    Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered encryption weaknesses in the updated HYFLOCK ransomware builds. The ransomware operation began to publicly name victims in October 2026, although evidence indicates that the group first appeared in underground forums in March 2026. As of writing, the group has listed 13 victims. "The October 17 build successfully encrypted files, registered a scheduled task, accessed network-share resources, and attempted to interfere with system recovery," Check Point said. "In an earlier October version, researchers identified a processing defect that could permanently discard portions of a file, potentially preventing complete recovery even with the correct decryption key. The October 17 build exhibited another issue. Larger files had only their first 4,096 bytes encrypted, leaving additional content accessible beyond that initial section."

  14. Customer Identity Data Accessed
    DigiCert Discloses Unauthorized Access to Business System

    DigiCert said it has identified an event involving unauthorized access to one of its business systems that stores information shared by customer representatives to validate their identity. The company said its certificate operations were not impacted. "Most of the data was limited to business contact information for customers: names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses," DigiCert said. "A small minority of customer accounts included additional personal data in the form of a customer-provided document such as a driver's license, passport, utility bill, or other document with name and address. The access could not write records, act as a validation approver, or issue certificates."

  15. DeFi Hijack Drains $138K
    Hackers Hijack DeFi Websites Registered with Name.com

    Threat actors have hijacked a little over a dozen DeFi websites registered with Name.com, including Flap, Kintsu, Pickle Finance and Origami Finance, ultimately stealing about $138,000 in assets. The sites have been found to be rigged with a malware kit that tricks visitors into approving transfers out of their wallets once they connect them to the compromised site. Vercel said it's aware of nine domains associated with the platform that were impacted. "Over about 45 minutes on Oct 31 (UTC), an account within an associated support team made changes to the nameservers associated with 15 domains registered with name.com," Name.com said in a post-mortem. "The domains were directed to a malicious page hosting Step Drainer malware."

  16. Stolen Cloud App Credentials Abused
    Malicious Entra Service Principal Sign-Ins Recorded

    Todyl has disclosed that an unknown threat actor has been abusing stolen Microsoft Entra ID application credentials and Azure DevOps identities to access MSPs' Microsoft 365 and Azure environments, reaching at least 27 organizations. "About 45 app registrations at roughly 18 organizations were targeted, and more than 33 of them authenticated successfully," Todyl said. "Through those apps the actor has reached 27 organizations so far, including the MSPs' downstream clients in government, energy, food and agriculture, transportation, construction and engineering, legal, education and nonprofits. It has run searches across about 25 tenants, downloaded 81 files and accessed around 2,279 mailbox items." The sign-in activity has originated from the IP address 199.19.77[.]84.

  17. Syrian Hacker Gets 42 Months
    Syrian Man Sentenced for Hacking Conspiracy

    Ahmad Umar Agha (aka Th3Pr0), a Syrian national tied to the Syrian Electronic Army (SEA), has been sentenced to 42 months in prison in the U.S. for his involvement in an expansive hacking conspiracy organized and led by members of former Syrian President Bashar Al-Assad regime between Aug 2011 and January 2014. "To spread the former Syrian government's propaganda, Agha hacked approximately 47 Western media entities, businesses, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and U.S. and allied government entities," the Justice Department said. "In one instance, Agha’s actions caused a flash crash in the U.S. stock market, resulting in a temporary $136 billion loss in the value of stocks making up the Dow Jones Industrial Average." Agha and his alleged accomplice, Firas Dardar, were first charged in June 2014. Dardar remains at large.

  18. Malicious AI Search Results Steal Crypto
    Stealing Crypto From Web-Browsing AI Agents

    A new piece of malware has been observed targeting AI agents creating cryptocurrency wallets. "A GitHub repository posing as a Solana starter kit, which ranks as the top result when an agent searches for one, contains malware that gives an attacker remote control of the victim's machine, including the crypto wallets on it," AIR Security said. The activity has been codenamed SolanaCry. The attack builds upon the foundation of Web Hole, where an AI agent, in its quest for finding answers to a problem, can inadvertently run a command suggested by an attacker and perform malicious actions. "To get a payload into search results, an attacker has two options," AIR said. "The first is to build a site of their own and grow its reputation with SEO, backlinks, content, time, until the search engine treats it as relevant and trusted. Once it ranks, they change the content and drop in the payload. The second is easier: find dead sites that still show up as ranked results, and use those to deliver it."

  19. Android Banking Malware Spreads
    Mirax Android RAT Targets META

    Thousands of Android phones belonging to retail banking customers in the Middle East, Turkey, and Africa (META) region have been compromised with the Mirax trojan between March and September 2026, leading to estimated losses worth millions of U.S. dollars. "Where unauthorized international transfers were reported, funds were sent to accounts abroad, some of which are suspected to be mule accounts," Group-IB said. "The campaign uses dynamically generated package names and impersonates 'Google Play Services' to evade user suspicion and signature-based detection." Like most Android malware, Mirax is used to facilitate device takeover (DTO) fraud by abusing Android's accessibility services. "With it, the attacker is able to see and control the compromised device in real time: reading credentials, intercepting one-time codes, capturing the PIN to unlock the device later, opening a banking app and moving money out to newly added beneficiaries and mule accounts abroad," Group-IB said. Campaigns using Mirax have been attributed to Aquafina, a threat actor known to be active since March 16, 2026.

  20. AI Model Bypasses Task Instructions
    GLM-5.3 Violates Instructions to Reach Correct Answers

    Irregular's evaluation of Zhipu AI's open-weight model GLM-5.3 across 13 offensive cyber scenarios using CyScenarioBench has found that the model "did not refuse any of the tested offensive tasks" and "repeatedly reached correct answers while violating explicit task instructions." The AI security company said these violations can be interpreted as a form of reward hacking. "Crediting the answer alone could mislead capability assessments and deployment decisions, while rewarding it during training could reinforce these instruction violations," it added.

One thing stands out this week: attackers don't always need to be smarter than the systems they're targeting. They just need to find what was missed, left open, or trusted a little too much. And with AI making some of that searching easier, the time between finding a problem and using it is getting shorter. How much damage can someone do without breaking much? Quite a lot, it seems. A stolen login can open doors across several systems. A trusted setting can be used to lock people out. Even a simple file copy can reach places it shouldn't. And while new tools are helping find security holes faster, some important systems are still taking months, sometimes over a year, to get patched. Not exactly a great match.

The stranger part is how little some attacks now need. Ransom demands without encrypted files. Fake websites that look real enough to steal money. AI tools picking up dangerous instructions while trying to help. Even the attackers are making mistakes in their own code.

This week's stories are a reminder that the biggest problems don't always come from clever tricks. Sometimes the easy way works just fine. Here's what else happened.

The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out.
  1. AI Accelerates Zero-Day Discovery
    NCSC Warns of AI-Enabled Attacks

    The U.K. National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) has warned that the widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has "almost certainly" led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities. "Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and have made patching a quicker process," NCSC said. "However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses. Additionally, an organisation’s internal patching and testing processes will need to evolve to meet the pace of accelerating vulnerability discovery. Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal."

  2. Critical Systems Face Prolonged Exposure
    Network Appliances Go More Than a Year Without Patches

    An analysis of roughly 383,000 CVEs disclosed from 1999 through September 2026 has found that the median time to patch a vulnerability exceeds a year for network appliances. About 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation. "The median vulnerability is patched in about two weeks on Windows workstations but in more than a month on Windows Servers," Microsoft said. "It stretches to 10+ weeks on Linux Servers and for applications running on macOS, and beyond a year on network appliances. That gap is the threat actor's window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest." The tech giant also said threat actors disproportionately target flaws that maximize impact and exposure and enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass.

  3. $4.5 Million Fraud Network Busted
    Investment Fraud Scheme Dismantled in Europe

    Authorities have arrested seven people allegedly involved in an investment fraud scheme that claimed potential victims in more than 50 countries, according to Europol. The operation caused estimated losses of at least $4.5 million. The "crime-as-a-service" offering was run by a company from Cyprus and Israel, and allegedly provided cybercrime groups with an assortment of trading websites and fraudulent call centers tasked with tricking victims into transferring their savings. These call centers operated from Albania, Kosovo, and North Macedonia. "More than 100 servers were seized and seven suspects arrested during coordinated action on 3 November 2026," Europol said. "Authorities searched 17 locations and seized servers, other evidence and assets." Like other fraudulent investment schemes, the operation leveraged deceptive advertisements to funnel people towards fraudulent investment platforms, promising them substantial, quick returns from cryptocurrency trading and foreign currencies. Although victims were encouraged to transfer a small amount, they displayed illusory gains to push them into transferring increasingly large sums. The operators resorted to delaying tactics to block payments when they attempted to withdraw their funds. "Behind seemingly legitimate platforms, supposed brokers used fictitious profits and sustained psychological pressure to persuade victims to invest more," Europol said. "Personal data collected through this process was sold to criminal groups operating call centers. Operators then contacted potential victims with supposed investment opportunities, turning their initial interest into repeated demands for money."

  4. $250K Bounty for Critical Cloud Flaws
    Google Expands Cloud Vulnerability Reward Program

    Google has expanded its Cloud Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) with a new top-tier reward for high-impact architectural security flaws, allowing researchers to earn $250,000 for Root-in-Cloud bugs, including tenant-isolation bypasses and complex cross-service logic flaws that let attackers gain full administrative control over arbitrary Google Cloud organizations. "To earn this premier reward, you must demonstrate full administrative control, the equivalent of 'roles/owner' or complete IAM control, over arbitrary Google Cloud organizations or projects with no prior access or special project setup," Google said. "Additionally, valid vulnerability reports demonstrating remote code execution (RCE) in underlying Google production infrastructure (Borg) or achieving root-in-prod will automatically be evaluated by the Google Cloud VRP panel for root-in-cloud eligibility."

  5. Edge Blocks Scam Notification Abuse
    Microsoft Takes on Notification Spam in Edge

    Microsoft has announced that its Edge browser will now automatically disable notifications from sites that push scam or scareware notifications, such as fake virus warnings or security alerts. "As of last month’s rollout of Edge 156, when Microsoft Defender SmartScreen or Scareware blocker detects a scam that was pushed through a notification, Edge will automatically disable notifications from the site that sent it," Microsoft said. "The next time Edge starts, an information bar explains what happened. If you believe a site was blocked incorrectly, you can review sites with blocked notifications and unblock them from Edge Settings, keeping you in control."

  6. University Cryptojacking Charges
    U.S. Charges Two Canadians for Hacking U.S. Universities

    Two Canadian men, Ryan James Roach, 35, and Mathiew James Stubbings, 41, have been indicted in the U.S. for hacking multiple U.S. universities and using the access to mine cryptocurrency. Both have been charged with conspiracy to obtain information from a protected computer and to cause damage to a protected computer, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentional damage to a protected computer, which carry a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. "Between June 2016, and December 2019, Roach and Stubbings conspired to engage in a scheme to hack into computers, steal login credentials, and secretly mine cryptocurrency for financial gain," the Justice Department said. "They used virtual private servers in multiple countries, which were registered under false names. These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials. Victims of the scheme included educational institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Massachusetts."

  7. Ransomware Extortion Without Encryption
    PAYLOAD Ransomware Weaponizes Active Directory GPO

    Cybersecurity researchers have detailed an encryptionless extortion attack involving PAYLOAD ransomware targeting a manufacturing organization in the Middle East. "The threat actor obtained domain admin-equivalent control of the organization’s Active Directory environment and authored a malicious Group Policy Object (GPO) named PAYLOAD, linking it at the domain root," Kaspersky said. "Through that single object, the actor delivered ransom notes, hijacked the desktop wallpaper and lock screen, enforced a logon banner, and disabled the local administrator account across every domain-joined Windows workstation — all without dropping a ransomware binary or encrypting any data. The only ransomware we found in this incident was a PAYLOAD sample targeting ESXi on Linux servers." The attack represents a convergence of two trends: Living-off-the-land abuse of trusted AD infrastructure and a surge in extortion-only incidents.

  8. AI Sandbox Escape Exposes Sensitive Files
    Docker Sandboxes Flaw Lets AI Agents Access and Overwrite Files Outside Isolated Workspaces

    A vulnerability impacting Docker Sandboxes (CVE-2026-103916) could have been exploited to bypass file access restrictions, potentially exposing cloud credentials and other sensitive files on a developer's machine through a routine copy command. "The command used to copy files between a sandbox and the developer's computer (sbx cp) does not enforce these access restrictions," Endor Labs said. "An agent can exploit this weakness using what is known as a symbolic link, essentially a shortcut that points to another file or folder. By placing a malicious shortcut inside an approved workspace, the agent can trick a subsequent copy command into accessing files outside the sandbox's approved boundaries." The issue has been addressed in Docker Sandboxes version 0.51.0.

  9. Smart TVs Keep Tracking After Opt-Out
    Does Opting Out of ACR Work?

    A new study has revealed that smart TVs running operating systems from Samsung, Vizio, and Roku continue to transmit data to automatic content recognition (ACR) endpoints even after users opt out of tracking in the devices' settings. "Opting out fully worked on only four operating systems. On Samsung and Vizio, traffic consistent with ACR kept flowing, and Roku's opt-out doesn't cover its own streaming service," according to a group of academics from Northeastern University. "VIDAA OS sends ACR data to servers run by Unruly over MQTT without encryption, so anyone on the network path between the TV and those servers can read it."

  10. Cryptographic Proof for AI Outputs
    Anthropic Unveils FlashProve Prototype

    Anthropic has revealed that it's working on an open-source system called FlashProve to cryptographically verify an AI response came from a given model. "FlashProve is a system for provable inference of large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models," Anthropic said. "FlashProve involves two parties: the model provider (the prover) and a user (the verifier). It is split into two phases: In the offline phase, the prover publishes a commitment to the model weights, which is a short fingerprint to pin down one exact choice of weights while the weights themselves remain hidden. The later inference claims will be checked against that commitment, i.e., the weight model committed to in this phase. In the online phase, upon requests from the verifier (i.e., prompts and the corresponding output tokens), the prover produces a proof file proving the following statement: The committed model produces these output tokens when evaluated. Anyone who holds the commitment, the prompt, and the reply can check it, without the weights and with limited compute power, and be convinced that the committed weights, run on this prompt, produce exactly these tokens."

DreamHost said the attacker may have accessed the credentials used to access the File Manager or webmail, along with the contents of emails and files in the FTP/SFTP server.   12. Pre-Auth RCE and Account Takeover

    The maintainers of Apache OFBiz have addressed 46 security flaws, including CVE-2026-68524, which could result in pre-authentication remote code execution, and CVE-2026-109928, which enables full account takeover due to an incorrect authentication algorithm implementation. The issues have been patched in Apache OFBiz 24.09.08.

  13. Ransomware Encryption Flaws Exposed

    Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered encryption weaknesses in the updated HYFLOCK ransomware builds. The ransomware operation began to publicly name victims in October 2026, although evidence indicates that the group first appeared in underground forums in March 2026. As of writing, the group has listed 13 victims. "The October 17 build successfully encrypted files, registered a scheduled task, accessed network-share resources, and attempted to interfere with system recovery," Check Point said. "In an earlier October version, researchers identified a processing defect that could permanently discard portions of a file, potentially preventing complete recovery even with the correct decryption key. The October 17 build exhibited another issue. Larger files had only their first 4,096 bytes encrypted, leaving additional content accessible beyond that initial section."

  14. Customer Identity Data Accessed
    DigiCert Discloses Unauthorized Access to Business System

    DigiCert said it has identified an event involving unauthorized access to one of its business systems that stores information shared by customer representatives to validate their identity. The company said its certificate operations were not impacted. "Most of the data was limited to business contact information for customers: names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses," DigiCert said. "A small minority of customer accounts included additional personal data in the form of a customer-provided document such as a driver's license, passport, utility bill, or other document with name and address. The access could not write records, act as a validation approver, or issue certificates."

  15. DeFi Hijack Drains $138K
    Hackers Hijack DeFi Websites Registered with Name.com

    Threat actors have hijacked a little over a dozen DeFi websites registered with Name.com, including Flap, Kintsu, Pickle Finance and Origami Finance, ultimately stealing about $138,000 in assets. item.title: Researchers Bypass ChatGPT Lockdown Mode to Exfiltrate Chats Without User Interaction (2026)
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a now-patched vulnerability that could be exploited to bypass Lockdown Mode protections in OpenAI ChatGPT.

Lockdown Mode was introduced by the artificial intelligence (AI) company in June 2026 as an optional setting to minimize data exfiltration risks arising from prompt injections.

"The flaw could enable silent chat data theft, phishing, and malware delivery, including zero-click data exfiltration in the ChatGPT desktop application," Eli Smadja, head of research at Check Point, said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The problem stems from HTML page previews inside ChatGPT code blocks, which allow HTML content to be rendered directly within the application. Given that executing user-supplied HTML and JavaScript can introduce security risks of its own, the content is placed inside a sandbox so that it cannot access data from the app, such as cookies and local storage.

The sandbox also prevents the rendered content from communicating with external resources without user consent. Lockdown Mode acts as a security barrier, mitigating data exfiltration risk by limiting outbound network requests that could be used to transfer sensitive information to an attacker-controlled infrastructure.

However, Check Point found a loophole in the manner popup windows are handled during HTML previews that made it possible to escape the confines of the sandbox and bypass Lockdown Mode.

"The HTML preview used nested sandboxed frames, and while ChatGPT intercepted direct attempts to open new windows, the underlying sandbox permissions still allowed popups and permitted them to escape the sandbox," Smadja explained. 

"By creating another nested frame within the rendered page, it was possible to access an unmodified popup function and bypass the restrictions placed on the original HTML preview. Content opened through this route was no longer subject to the same sandbox restrictions, providing a way to circumvent the protections of Lockdown Mode."

Once the restrictions are bypassed, a threat actor can exploit the vulnerability to exfiltrate data, chat messages, or deliver malicious payloads by means of a crafted prompt, a malicious GPT, or a shared chat.

What's more, as the attacker is in complete control of the content displayed in the popup window, it could be used to render convincing social-engineering lures, such as a fake ChatGPT update, and trick the victim into downloading malware by persuading them to click on a link.

That said, the underlying issue is not limited to the Electron-based desktop environment, highlighting how weakness outside of the scope of the AI model can undermine AI security controls. Following responsible disclosure, the vulnerability was addressed by OpenAI on September 18, 2026.

"Lockdown Mode was specifically intended to reduce the possibility of data leaving a conversation through potentially malicious outbound requests, yet a weakness in another application feature provided an alternative path around that security boundary," Smadja said.

"The finding raises a broader enterprise security issue: AI security controls are only as strong as the wider application environment around them."

The disclosure comes a week after Parameter Labs detailed a way to bypass ChatGPT's sandbox and content security policy (CSP) and take over anyone's account simply by sending an attacker-controlled public ChatGPT share link and prompting them to click the HTML preview once. If the HTML block is marked as previewable, it's opened automatically.

"An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user," security researcher Mukul Goyal said. "When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt[.]com with access to the victim's authenticated web session."

Check Point told The Hacker News that the two shortcomings are different vulnerabilities on the same component, with the takeover bug enabling Javascript code execution outside of the sandbox so as to make the victim call out chatgpt[.]com and perform API requests on behalf of the victim

"This demonstrates how every new feature is a chance for more vulnerabilities," the company said in a statement.

Earlier this September, Check Point also demonstrated a covert cross-account command channel through which an attacker could use a victim's ChatGPT session to run hidden tasks with the tools, data, and connected apps available to that session, alongside the visible conversation.

"The victim could receive a normal answer to their visible request while the attacker's task was processed separately and its result returned across accounts," Check Point said. "The channel operated through code-execution environments belonging to different ChatGPT accounts."

"The hidden instruction could be delivered through a malicious prompt, a shared ChatGPT conversation, or a custom GPT. Once it was present in the victim's conversation context, an ordinary message could trigger the attacker-controlled task without revealing it in the visible response."

The findings coincide with the discovery of a number of security shortcomings in various AI-driven tools and services over the past few months to trick them into spilling secrets or carrying out unauthorized actions -

  • An attack called SkillJacking that hijacks dependencies used by skills (repositories, packages, domains, or cloud apps) to compromise every agent installing them.
  • A set of vulnerabilities in built-in browsers associated with five AI coding assistants, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Visual Studio Code, and Anthropic Claude Desktop that could be exploited to execute code on a host machine, read and steal files, or spoof web browser address bars. The issues have been codenamed Embrace, short for EMbedded BRowser - Arbitrary Code Execution, Arbitrary Content Exfiltration, and Arbitrary Context Emulation.
  • A technique called Repeat-After-Me that targets LangChain LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, Microsoft AutoGen, Google Agent Development Kit 2.0, AWS Strands Agents, and CrewAI and tricks them into running tool calls by means of a "seemingly benign text-repetition request."
  • A vulnerability called AgentCorruption that could allow an attacker to interact with an exposed AI agent running on AWS Bedrock AgentCore and leverage prompt injection techniques to influence that agent and extract its IMDS credentials, and then use them to access other agents, read private conversations, steal connected-tool credentials, and manipulate agent behavior.
  • A vulnerability in SpaceXSI Grok and GitHub Copilot CLI called Cryptographic Context Injection that could be exploited to read a developer's local files and send them to an external server from a single web page via an indirect prompt injection, which hides malicious instructions inside AES-encrypted text.
  • A zero-click vulnerability called SalesBleed that could be exploited to extract sensitive account data out of Salesforce Agentforce by leveraging the Web-to-Lead form to plant an indirect prompt injection payload.
  • A proof-of-concept (PoC) attack called not-a-mused that allows an unprivileged local attacker (or process) to redirect Meta Muse's dictation traffic and abuse the permissions granted to the AI assistant to perform arbitrary actions.
  • A zero-click vulnerability called Plugin4Shell that could be exploited to conduct an AI supply chain attack by silently swapping a trusted plugin with a malicious one while bypassing SHA pinning. "The agent checks out the exact commit the marketplace pinned but never verifies it landed there, so an attacker who controls the plugin's repo makes the checkout resolve to malicious code while the pin still looks honored," Air Security said. "The result is zero-click remote code execution across Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini CLI."
  • An attack called BragJack that can be exploited to hijack the AI agents built into browsers like Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Opera Neon, Perplexity Comet, and Anthropic Claude in Chrome by using an already installed malicious browser extension in conjunction with prompt forcing.
  • A behavioral effect called sampling drift demonstrates how adding an invisible watermark to a large language model's (LLM) output can unintentionally change how the model behaves, including the tools an AI agent invokes, and likely weaken safety refusals. "Watermarking changes refusal behavior on bare harmful requests, but the effect is more pronounced when the same requests are paired with the prompt-injection technique," Lasso Security said. "On several models, watermarking then makes the model more likely to answer harmful requests that it would otherwise refuse."
  • A set of attacks that exploit customer support AI agents to compose and send phishing emails, invoke tool calls, and bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) protections.
  • A prompt-crafting technique called PuzzleMask that bypasses quick LLM-based policy checks carried out by a lightweight gatekeeper model by planting the malicious instruction in a specially crafted prose wrapper, after which the payload is processed by a more powerful target model to trigger malicious actions.
  • A technique called Workflow Identity Hijacking allows an attacker to bypass standard controls by sending normal, benign requests through an unauthenticated entry point, causing the enterprise AI pipeline to process the request and execute the action as designed. "The core failure is that the requester had no authority to make that request," Noma Security said. "When an AI workflow performs downstream actions, it executes using high-privilege service accounts or developer API keys rather than enforcing the permissions of the external user. As a result, AI workflows become unauthenticated proxies for privileged actions and silent data exfiltration."
  • A zero-click vulnerability class called PleaseFix that could be exploited to hijack AI agents embedded in agentic browsers by placing malicious instructions inside emails, calendar invitations, or web pages, and exploit a technique referred to as intent collision to cause the agent to "act on the attacker's behalf using the user's own identity, permissions and access."
  • A set of vulnerabilities impacting AI coding agents from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI that could be exploited to trick them into handing over a victim's secrets, achieving persistent instruction poisoning by modifying the AGENTS.md file, and compromising software releases through prompt injections placed inside untrusted user inputs, like GitHub issues.

"Agents are becoming the default infrastructure across CI/CD, messaging, triage, incident response, and support," Novee Security said. "The more autonomous they get, the more the harness decides what's safe on your behalf, and the more untrusted input reaches real execution."

item.title: OpenSSH Issues Emergency Fix for Flaw Letting Long Passwords Bypass SSH Auth on Alpine Linux (2026)
item.description:
Attackers can log in to accounts that have no password, such as SSH key-only accounts, on some Alpine Linux servers running the standard openssh-server package. They need network access to the server, an account name, and a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long.

OpenSSH, which rates the flaw critical, released version 10.6p2 today to block it. Alpine has published fixed packages for every release back to 3.16.

The attack works when the OpenSSH server (sshd) checks passwords without the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface, password logins are enabled, and at least one other account on the machine has a password. Alpine's openssh-server package is built without PAM, and password logins are on by default.

The flaw comes from how sshd works with musl, the C library that Alpine is built on. Non-Linux systems, Linux systems built on glibc, and systems that check passwords through PAM are not affected, said Damien Miller of the OpenSSH project.

He told anyone running an affected system to "set PasswordAuthentication=no or disable SSH for these systems IMMEDIATELY." No attacks using the flaw have been reported.

Who Is Exposed

Alpine's security advisory lists four conditions. A server is exposed when all four are true:

  • It runs the openssh-server package, which is built without PAM, or runs openssh-server-pam with UsePAM no.
  • PasswordAuthentication is yes, which is the OpenSSH default.
  • An account has * as its password field, which means no password is set.
  • At least one other local account has a password hash starting with $5$ or $6$.

The attacker also needs the name of an account with no password. One account with a password is enough to expose every account without one. The attack succeeds on every try with a single connection, according to the advisory.

On Alpine, accounts with no password set include:

  • key-only users created with adduser without a password, or with usermod -p '*'
  • users who come from a directory service through musl-nscd, since they have no shadow entry
  • root, which has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16
  • the alpine user in the official cloud images built with tiny-cloud

Root is protected by the default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password setting and can be reached directly only if PermitRootLogin yes is set. That protection does not help if an exposed account can become root, for example through doas.

The tiny-cloud images from 3.18.11 through 3.24.3 give the alpine user passwordless doas. They are safe at first boot but become open to attack once any $6$ hash exists on the machine, for example after an admin sets a console password. An attacker can then log in as alpine and use doas to become root.

Containers that do not run sshd, systems with PasswordAuthentication no, and cloud images set up through cloud-init, which writes that setting, are not affected. Accounts locked with ! in /etc/shadow are not affected either, and neither are machines where no account has a $-style password hash.

The flaw is not limited to Alpine. Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield, who reported it, names OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto in his technical write-up as other musl-based systems to check.

OpenWrt handles SSH with Dropbear by default, as its Dropbear documentation shows, and Kültekin says Dropbear is not affected. On OpenWrt, the flaw can matter only where an admin has installed the OpenSSH server.

How to Fix It

On Alpine, the fix is a package update followed by a restart, because upgrading the package does not restart the running sshd:

  1. Update the packages: apk upgrade -U -a
  2. Restart the server: rc-service sshd restart

Point releases 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 already include the fixed package. Branches 3.16 to 3.21 are past their end of support but also got fixed packages.

Cloud instances started from tiny-cloud images older than those point releases still need the update, or the setting below.

If you build OpenSSH yourself, version 10.6p2 includes the change, as its release notes describe.

If you cannot update yet, turning off password logins also stops the attack. First make sure your SSH key login works, and keep your current session open until a new login succeeds. Then set PasswordAuthentication no, check the configuration with sshd -t, and restart sshd.

The advisory gives commands that add the setting in a drop-in file in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d, which Alpine's default configuration reads from 3.19 onward. They also change every PasswordAuthentication line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config from yes to no, including lines inside a Match block. Afterward, sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication should print passwordauthentication no.

The advisory suggests looking in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password, such as alpine, root or a key-only user. On exposed machines, also review doas use, recently created users, files and authorized keys.

"If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised," it says.

Why Long Passwords Work

Without PAM, sshd checks a password itself. It hashes the attempt with crypt(), the C library function that turns a password into its stored form, and compares the result with the stored field.

An account with no password has only * in that field. That is too short to hold a salt, the random prefix of a hash, so sshd borrows the salt of another account that has a real hash.

For the $5$ and $6$ hash types, musl's crypt() refuses passwords longer than 256 bytes and returns * to signal the error. That * matches the stored *, so sshd accepts the login. The upper end of the range is sshd's own limit of 1,024 bytes per password.

This behavior comes from a musl change on August 9, 2012, which made a failed crypt() call return "an unmatchable hash rather than NULL" because many programs did not check for failure. The 256-byte limit followed on August 29, 2012, to protect servers from denial-of-service attacks.

The salt borrowing comes from a July 15, 2016, OpenSSH change that addressed CVE-2016-6210, a flaw that let attackers learn which usernames exist. Kültekin says the problem has existed since then.

The 10.6p2 code change makes sshd refuse a match when the stored field is shorter than four characters. OpenSSH calls it a workaround and says the root cause lies outside sshd. Stable Alpine packages carry a patch for the same problem.

Why the Fix Came the Next Day

Miller's team learned of the flaw earlier this week and shipped the fix as fast as it could. In the release announcement, he said the team now sees long embargoes as dangerous and mainly helpful to attackers, because it has recently seen AI agents find the same bugs again, sometimes within hours.

No CVE identifier had been assigned to the flaw as of today.

item.title: Experts Demonstrate Barracuda Email Security Gateway Chain Enabling Root Access Without Login (2026)
item.description:
Two flaws in Barracuda's Email Security Gateway, an email-filtering appliance, can be chained to run commands on it as root, its highest level of access, with no login required.

The company released patches on Monday, and the security firm watchTowr detailed the attack chain on Thursday.

One flaw, CVE-2026-116606, is an authorization bypass. An unauthenticated attacker can use it to restore a crafted configuration backup and change the appliance's global settings.

The other, CVE-2026-111560, is a command injection. It runs commands as root but normally needs an administrator account, and on the Email Security Gateway the bypass gives an attacker that access. Chained, the two let an attacker reach root with no login.

Affected Products and Fixes

The authorization bypass affects only the Email Security Gateway. The command injection reaches five other products, but on those it still needs an administrator account.

Mandiant, which assigned the two CVE records, rates the bypass 9.3 out of 10 and the command injection 8.6. Barracuda has released a patch for each affected product and lists the fixed firmware in its security advisory. The Email Security Gateway is fixed in version 9.4.0.030 and later.

What to Do

The advisory sets out three steps:

  • Apply the patch for each affected product, or upgrade to the fixed firmware listed above.
  • If you cannot patch at once, limit the appliance's administration interface to trusted internal networks.
  • If you have turned automatic patching off, switch it back on.

How the Chain Works

In its technical analysis, watchTowr traced the chain through the appliance's code. A failed password change returns the attacker a low-privilege role instead of stopping the request, which leaves a backup-restore function open to someone who has not logged in.

That function accepts an uploaded backup, and the restored data includes a timezone value that the appliance later runs as a shell command with root privileges. Barracuda guards backups with a checksum, but the secret used to compute it is built into the code, allowing an attacker to forge a valid checksum. The firm showed the attack by writing a file to the appliance as root.

As of this week, neither flaw appears in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV catalog), and no public report ties either to an attack. watchTowr also released a detection tool that checks whether an appliance is vulnerable, but has not published an exploit.

The Email Security Gateway was hit in the 2023 attacks by a group tracked as UNC4841, which exploited a different flaw, CVE-2023-2868, as a zero-day. That case is unrelated to the two flaws patched this week, and nothing ties the new pair to any attacker.

item.title: Hackers Hide Linux Backdoor in Control Web Panel Server to Execute Commands Without Logs (2026)
item.description:
A backdoor has been found hiding in the web server that runs Control Web Panel (CWP), a free panel for managing Linux hosting servers, researchers at QiAnXin's XLab said this week.

The backdoored web server executes commands that attackers send via web requests, and those requests never appear in its access logs. Installing it takes root access, so the attackers must already control the server.

The researchers, who named the backdoor cwpdoor, captured its installer, a shell script posing as a version update, on June 29. The installer handles only two versions of that web server, cwpsrv 1.15.10 and 1.24.0. The researchers do not yet know how attackers get the root access the installer needs.

On September 30, an archive holding a copy of the backdoor was uploaded to VirusTotal from Brazil. The researchers say this indicates that "real victims already exist in the wild." They give no count of infected servers.

The backdoor is cwpsrv itself, rebuilt with extra code, the researchers found in their technical analysis. It behaves like the normal program until a request arrives with a valid timestamp and signature in custom headers whose names begin with X-Ngx-Integrity. It then runs the command carried in the request.

When the installer replaces the cwpsrv file, it puts the file's dates back to their original values, so checks with ls and stat show it as unchanged. When the researchers checked, the backdoor file had zero detections out of 63 on VirusTotal.

Checking a Server for the Backdoor

XLab gives three checks:

  • Socket: run ss -axp | grep integrity. A result naming ngx_http_integrity_helper, the Unix socket the backdoor uses, is a sign of infection.
  • Process: run ps aux | grep cwpsrv and look for unexpected helper processes started by cwpsrv.
  • File: run strings /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin/cwpsrv | grep X-Ngx-Integrity and look for the backdoor's header names.

In the researchers' example, the socket check found the backdoor on a server where the list of open ports looked normal.

The researchers published these indicators:

  • MD5: e505d4ffa21cf494a5dc2d7c8f4f1236 (installer script, cwpsrv_update.sh)
  • MD5: 965aea67fb40de1bab5169ada993349f (backdoored cwpsrv 1.15.10)
  • MD5: d3f4e95113d49ab3991b45e457bda75b (backdoored cwpsrv 1.24.0)
  • IP: 136.0.141[.]71 (download server)
  • URL: http://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_update.sh
  • URL: http://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_1.15.10
  • URL: http://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_1.24.0

Cleaning Up an Infected Server

If a server is infected, the researchers recommend three steps:

  1. Restore the original cwpsrv from the backup the installer creates in /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin, with a name starting cwpsrv.prev- and ending in a date and time. The researchers' description of the installer says it deletes "the temporary files and backup" after a successful swap, so this copy may be missing.
  2. Upgrade to the latest version, then confirm that ss -axp | grep integrity returns nothing.
  3. Change all control panel credentials, because the backdoor can run any command. Treat the whole server as compromised and check it for other threats.

The archive uploaded from Brazil also held the Ebury malware, an OpenSSH backdoor and credential stealer active since at least 2009. The researchers do not know whether the two are related, and say different attackers may have planted them on the same server.

item.title: Chainalysis Breach Exposes All Users' Credentials, Forces Shutdown of Key Services (2026)
item.description:
Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis has revealed that its ongoing investigation into the agentic cyber attack targeting its systems also exposed names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all users.

"While we investigated, we removed access to Reactor and Data Solutions," the company said. "At this time we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated."

Chainalysis said it has implemented additional proactive monitoring systems to detect unusual activity, adding it took the Know Your Transaction (KYT) user interface and API offline, alongside other address screening products and the login page.

Out of an abundance of caution, Chainalysis has also taken the step of locking the impacted accounts.

  • 38.246.114.118
  • 104.243.32.50
  • 31.57.201.201
